issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' is hard to reconcile with simultaneously becoming so overwhelmed on recall that she has to stop and experiencing intense rage when remembering. Mild coexistence is possible, but 'very easily' directly opposes marked emotional disorganization on recall and is clinically inconsistent within the same node.

issues.item: Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy 'Avoid Police' is poorly aligned with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a combat trauma in a 21-year-old nurse, avoidance of police is not supported by the listed triggers, threat items, or memory content, which center on sirens, bodily arousal, transport, flashbacks, scanning, and rage/overwhelm. This looks like a strategy targeting a threat context not otherwise represented in the formulation or symptom profile.

Avoiding police is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile for a combat trauma survivor who is a nurse. The other selected items center on alarm, flashbacks, sirens, somatic arousal, and generalized danger scanning, but nothing else suggests police-specific threat, authority-related trauma meaning, or a law-enforcement context. This strategy appears disconnected from the trigger, threat, and memory content.

Bus riding as a selected trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it lacks a clear clinical link to the other chosen items. The active formulation strongly links triggers with threat and maladaptive strategies, yet the other trigger items are sirens and heart racing, and the threat/memory items emphasize flashbacking, rage, overwhelm, and danger scanning without any transport-related cueing. As selected here, this item feels insufficiently anchored to the rest of the combat-related profile.

vignette:
Leilani was twenty-one, a nurse, and she had been home from her deployment for eleven months when the sirens started following her. The first time was on a Tuesday afternoon, driving home from the hospital; an ambulance passed her on the highway, and she was suddenly back in the forward operating base, the air-raid warning screaming overhead. Her heart slammed against her ribs, and her hands locked on the steering wheel so hard that her knuckles went white. She had to pull over. She sat there shaking, the sound of the siren fading into the distance, but the feeling of it-the certainty that something was about to explode-stayed with her for hours.

The memory of that day in the combat zone came back not as a story she could tell, but as a wave of rage and overwhelm that rose up without warning. She had been on a routine supply run when the mortar hit. The blast, the dust, the screaming. She remembered the medic beside her, the way his face went slack. She remembered the rage. It was a hot, helpless fury at the enemy, at the command who had sent them through that corridor, at herself for not seeing it coming. When the memory returned, she felt so overwhelmed by emotion that she had to stop whatever she was doing. She knew what had happened, but she could not find the words to describe it. The words simply were not there.

The rage was the hardest part. It did not stay in the past. It leaked into the present. A loud noise-a car backfiring, a door slamming-and she would be on her feet, fists clenched, ready to fight someone who was not there. Her boyfriend, Marcus, learned not to startle her. He learned to announce himself before entering a room. Even so, there were evenings when she snapped at him for no reason, her voice sharp and cruel, and she saw the hurt in his face before she could take it back. She hated that. She hated herself for it. But the scanning for danger was constant now, and it wore her out. She could not stop checking her surroundings, could not stop watching the faces of strangers in the parking lot, could not stop listening for the wrong sound in the silence.

She began to avoid things that might make her feel happy or hopeful. It was not a conscious decision at first, but she noticed that whenever she let herself relax-a movie with Marcus, a walk in the park-the crash afterward was worse. The happiness felt like a trap. So she stopped. She stopped making plans. She stopped saying yes to invitations. She also stopped exercising, even though she had been a runner before the deployment. The first time she tried to jog after coming home, her heart started pounding, and the pounding felt exactly like the seconds before the mortar hit. She could not separate the sensation from the memory. So she stopped running.

The scanning for danger made everything worse. Every time she caught herself checking a room, every time she flinched at a siren, the memory of the attack came back stronger. It was as if the hypervigilance itself was the trigger, a feedback loop that tightened with each rotation. The more she scanned, the more she remembered. The more she remembered, the more she scanned. She could not break it. The rage and the overwhelm fed on each other, and the scanning fed on both. She started to believe that if she stopped watching, something terrible would happen. That she would be caught off guard again. That the next explosion would not miss.

The sirens were everywhere. She worked at a hospital in the city, and ambulances came and went all day. Every siren was a hook that pulled her out of the present and dropped her back into the dust and the noise. She began to dread her shifts. She avoided the emergency department entrance. She took the long way around the building, even though it made her late. She could not explain it to her supervisor. She could not explain it to anyone. She just knew that the sound undid her, and that the undoing was getting faster, not slower.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment in the break room. A coworker dropped a metal tray, and Leilani was on the floor, her back against the wall, her hands over her ears, her heart pounding so hard she thought she might die. She did not remember getting there. She did not remember the seconds in between. She only knew that she could not keep living this way-that the rage and the fear and the scanning and the memory had become a cage she could not find the door to. She was terrified that she was losing herself. She was terrified that Marcus would leave. She was terrified that the next time a siren went off, she would not come back.
